'''''Melaleuca quinquenervia''''', commonly known as the '''broad-leaved paperbark''' or '''paper bark tea tree''' in Australia, '''niaouli''' in New Caledonia and '''punk tree''' in the United States,  is a small- to medium-sized tree of the myrtle [[Family (taxonomy)|family]], [[Myrtaceae]]. It grows as a spreading tree up to {{convert|20|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} tall, with its trunk covered by a white, beige and grey thick papery bark. The grey-green leaves are egg-shaped, and cream or white bottlebrush-like flowers appear from late spring to autumn. It was first formally described in 1797 by the [[Spaniards|Spanish]] naturalist [[Antonio José Cavanilles]].

Native to [[New Caledonia]], [[Papua New Guinea]] and coastal eastern [[Australia]], from [[Botany Bay]] in [[New South Wales]] northwards into [[Queensland]], ''M. quinquenervia'' grows in swamps, on floodplains and near rivers and estuaries, often on silty soil.

==Description==
''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' is a small to medium sized, spreading tree which usually grows to a height of {{convert|8-15|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} high and a spread of {{convert|5-10|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} but is sometimes as tall as {{convert|25|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}}. The bark is papery and layers peels off in strips. Young growth is hairy with long and short, soft hairs. The leaves are arranged alternately and are flat, leathery, lance-shaped to egg-shaped, dull or grey-green, {{convert|55-120|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=in}} long and {{convert|10-31|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=in}} wide, three to eight times as long as wide, and have five prominent veins, referred to in its species name.<ref name=Brophy>{{cite book|last1=Brophy|first1=Joseph J.|last2=Craven|first2=Lyndley A.|last3=Doran|first3=John C.|title=Melaleucas: their botany, essential oils and uses|date=2013|publisher=Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research|location=Canberra|isbn=978-1-922137-51-7|pages=302–303}}</ref><ref name=Holliday>{{cite book|last1=Holliday|first1=Ivan|title=Melaleucas: a field and garden guide|date=2004|publisher=Reed New Holland Publishers|location=Frenchs Forest, N.S.W.|isbn=1-876334-98-3|pages=238–239|edition=2nd}}</ref><ref name="Wrigley">{{cite book|last1=Wrigley|first1=John W.|last2=Fagg|first2=Murray|title=Bottlebrushes, paperbarks & tea trees, and all other plants in the Leptospermum alliance|date=1993|publisher=Angus & Robertson|location=Pymble, N.S.W.|isbn=0-207-16867-9|page=297}}</ref><ref name="plantnet">{{cite web|last1=Wilson|first1=Peter G.|title=''Melelauca quinquenervia''|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Melaleuca~quinquenervia|publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney: plantnet|access-date=5 February 2017}}</ref><ref name="AustPlants">{{cite web|last1=Sheather|first1=Warren|last2=Sheather|first2=Gloria|last3=Clarke|first3=Dan|title=''Melelauca quinquenervia'' - Broad-leaved Paperbark|url=https://resources.austplants.com.au/plant/melaleuca-quinquenervia/|publisher=Australian Plants Society NSW|date=25 May 2020|access-date=17 March 2026}}</ref>

The flowers are arranged in spikes on the ends of branches which continue to grow after flowering, sometimes also in the upper leaf axils. The spikes contain 5 to 18 groups of flowers in threes and are up to {{convert|40|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} in diameter and {{convert|20-50|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long. The petals are about {{convert|3|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and fall off as the flower ages. The [[stamen]]s are white, cream-coloured or greenish and are arranged in 5 bundles around the flower, with 5 to 10 stamens per bundle. Flowering occurs from spring to early autumn, September to March in Australia. Flowering is followed by fruit which are woody, broadly cylindrical [[Capsule (botany)|capsules]], {{convert|2.5-4|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and clustered, spike-like along the branches. Each capsule contains many tiny seeds which are released annually.<ref name="Brophy" /><ref name="Holliday" /><ref name="Wrigley" /><ref name="plantnet" /><ref name=EJ93>{{cite book|author1=Elliot, Rodger W. |author2=Jones, David L. |author3=Blake. Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation:Volume 6 – K-M|year=1993 |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne |isbn=0-85091-589-9|page=359}}</ref>[[File:Melaleuca quinquenervia forest.jpg|thumb|225px|Habit near [[Woolgoolga, New South Wales|Woolgoolga]]]]

==Taxonomy==
The broad-leaved paperbark was first formally [[species description|described]] in 1797 by the Spanish naturalist [[Antonio José Cavanilles]], who gave it the name ''Metrosideros quinquenervia''. The description was of a specimen collected "near [[Port Jackson]]" and it was published in ''[[Icones et Descriptiones Plantarum]]''.<ref name=APNI(1)>{{cite web|title=''Metrosideros quinquenervia''|url=  https://biodiversity.org.au/boa/instance/apni/473477|publisher=APNI|access-date=23 July 2015}}</ref><ref name="Cav.">{{cite book|last1=Cavanilles|first1=Antonio Jose|title=Icones et Descriptiones Plantarum (Volume 4, No. 1)|date=1797|location=Madrid|page=19|url=http://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/spa/Libro.php?Libro=241|access-date=5 February 2017}}</ref> In 1958, [[Stanley Thatcher Blake]] of the [[Queensland Herbarium]] transferred the species to ''[[Melaleuca]]''.<ref name=APNI(2)>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca quinquenervia''|url=  https://biodiversity.org.au/boa/instance/apni/543006|publisher=APNI|access-date=23 July 2015}}</ref>  The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''quinquenervia'') is from the [[Latin]] ''quinque'' meaning "five" and ''nervus'', "vein", referring to the leaves usually having five veins.<ref name="Brophy" /><ref name="Wrigley" />

The common names broad-leaved paperbark, broad-leaved tea tree or simply paperbark or tea tree are used in Australia, and punk tree is used in the United States.<ref name=EJ93/> It is known as niaouli, itachou (paicî) and pichöö (xârâcùù) in [[New Caledonia]].<ref name="endemia">{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca quinquenervia''|url=http://endemia.nc/flore/fiche445.html|publisher=Endemia, New Caledonia|access-date=5 February 2017}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Melaleuca quinquenervia in Australia.jpg|thumb|''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' in Australia]] 
In Australia, ''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' occurs along the east coast, from [[Cape York Peninsula|Cape York]] in Queensland to Botany Bay in [[New South Wales]]. It grows in seasonally inundated plains and swamps, along estuary margins and is often the dominant species. In the [[Sydney]] region it grows alongside trees such as swamp mahogany (''[[Eucalyptus robusta]]'') and bangalay (''[[Eucalyptus botryoides|E. botryoides]]''). It grows in silty or swampy soil and plants have grown in acid soil of pH as low as 2.5.<ref name=Ben98>{{cite journal|last=Benson |first=Doug |author2=McDougall, Lyn |year=1998 |title=Ecology of Sydney plant species:Part 6 Dicotyledon family Myrtaceae |journal=Cunninghamia |volume=5 |issue=4 |page=969 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/269917#page/195/mode/1up}}</ref>

Broad-leaved paperbark is also [[Indigenous (ecology)|native]] in the southern part of [[Western New Guinea|West Papua]] and Papua New Guinea. It is widespread in New Caledonia, including [[Grande Terre (New Caledonia)|Grand Terre]], [[Bélep|Belep]], [[Isle of Pines (New Caledonia)|Isle of Pines]] and [[Maré Island|Maré]].<ref name="endemia" /> It is a component of the [[savannah]] of western New Caledonia, scattered trees dotting the grassland habitat and its spread through this landscape might have been facilitated by human fire regimes.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Dieter Mueller-Dombois |author2=Francis Raymond Fosberg |title=Vegetation of the tropical Pacific islands|publisher=Springer|year=1998|page=159|isbn=0-387-98313-9|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7UB5d33i8WkC&q=Niaouli+melaleuca+new+caledonia&pg=PA159|access-date=17 March 2011}}</ref> Major threats to ''M. quinquenervia'' are housing developments, roads, sugar cane and pine plantations. Remnants in Australia are not protected in reserves, with majority of its woodland located in private property where clearing continues.<ref name="TURNER">{{cite journal |last1=Turner |first1=Charles E. |last2=Center |first2=T.D. |last3=Burrows |first3=D.W. |last4=Buckingham |first4=G.R. |title=Ecology and management of ''Melaleuca quinquenervia'', an invader of wetlands in Florida, U.S.A. |journal=Wetlands Ecology and Management |date=1997 |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=165–178 |doi=10.1023/A:1008205122757|bibcode=1997WetEM...5..165T }}</ref>

''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' has been introduced as an [[ornamental plant]] to many tropical areas of the world, including [[Southeast Asia]], [[Africa]] and the [[Americas]] and has become a weed in many areas.<ref name="cabi">{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' (paperbark tree)|url=http://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/34348|publisher=Centre for Agriculture and Biosciences International|access-date=5 February 2017}}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' resprouts vigorously from [[epicormic shoot]]s after [[Bushfires in Australia|bushfire]], and has been recorded flowering within weeks of being burnt. Trees can live for over 100 years, with 40-year-old trees achieving a trunk circumference of {{convert|2.7|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} in cultivation.<ref name=Ben98/>

The flowers serve as a rich source of [[nectar]] for other organisms, including fruit bats, a wide range of insect and bird species,<ref name=EJ93/> such as the [[scaly-breasted lorikeet]] (''Trichoglossus chlorolepidotus'').<ref name="Lepschi">{{cite journal |last1=Lepschi |first1=Brendan J. |title=Food of Some Birds in Eastern New South Wales: Additions to Barker & Vestjens |journal=Emu |date=1991 |volume=93 |issue=3 |pages=195–199 |doi=10.1071/MU9930195 }}</ref>

The [[grey-headed flying fox]] (''Pteropus poliocephalus'') and [[little red flying-fox]] (''P. scapulatus'') consume the flowers.<ref>{{cite book |author=Eby P | year =1995| title =The biology and management of flying foxes in NSW | publisher = National Parks & Wildlife Service|location=Hurstville, NSW}}</ref>

===Status in the United States===
[[File:Melaleuca quinquenervia distribution in florida.jpg|thumb|''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' distribution in Florida]]
''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' was introduced into Florida as early as 1900 when specimens were first planted near [[Orlando, Florida|Orlando]].<ref name="MESKIMEN">{{citation |last=Meskimen |first=G. F. |title=A silvical study of the melaleuca tree in south Florida |type=thesis |year=1962 |publisher=Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences, University of Florida |location=Gainesville |pages=1–177 |url=https://tame.ifas.ufl.edu/pdfs/publications/Meskimen_1962.pdf}}</ref> There were two major introductions, one by J. Gifford to the East Coast in 1907, and one by A.C. Andrews to the west coast in 1912.<ref>{{cite news|last=Rothra|first=E.O.|title=John Clayton Gifford on preserving tropical Florida|newspaper=Miami Press, Coral Gables|year=1972}}</ref> The [[South Florida Water Management District]] has recorded ''Melaleuca'' around the areas where they were originally introduced: southwest of [[Broward County, Florida|Broward]] and northern [[Miami-Dade County, Florida|Dade County]] on the east coast and southern [[Lee County, Florida|Lee County]] and north of [[Collier County, Florida|Collier County]] on the west coast.<ref name="Wheeler">{{cite journal |last1=Wheeler |first1=Gregory S. |last2=Ordung |first2=K.M. |title=Lack of an induced response following fire and herbivory of two chemotypes of Melaleuca quinquenervia and its effect on two biological control agents |journal=Biological Control |date=2006 |volume=39 |issue=2 |pages=154–161 |doi=10.1016/j.biocontrol.2006.05.016 |bibcode=2006BiolC..39..154W }}</ref>

The species is mainly found in the more frost-free areas of south Florida and only rarely in the warmer coastal areas of [[Pasco County, Florida|Pasco County]].<ref name="ifas">{{cite web|last1=Jarvis|first1=BobbiJo|title=''Melaleuca'' – An Invasive Tree of Florida|url=http://pasco.ifas.ufl.edu/gardening/melaleuca.shtml|publisher=University of Florida – Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences|access-date=5 February 2017}}</ref>

''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' has been classified by the United States Department of Agriculture as a noxious weed in six US states (Florida, South Carolina, North Carolina, Massachusetts, Oklahoma and Texas), as well as federally.<ref name=USDA>{{GRIN | accessdate=6 February 2009}}</ref> It is an abundant [[List of invasive species in the Everglades|exotic invasive plant in the Everglades]].<ref name="Serbesoff-King">{{cite journal |last1=Serbesoff-King |first1=Kristina |title=''Melaleuca'' in Florida: A Literature Review on the Taxonomy, Distribution, Biology, Ecology, Economic Importance and Control Measures |journal=Journal of Aquatic Plant Management |date=2003 |volume=41 |issue=2 |pages=98–112 |url=https://apms.org/wp-content/uploads/japm-41-02-098.pdf |access-date=19 October 2024}}</ref> Its unchecked expansion in South Florida is one of the most serious threats to the integrity of the native [[ecosystem]].<ref name="Laroche">{{cite journal |last1=Laroche |first1=Francois B. |last2=Ferriter |first2=A.P. |title=The Rate of Expansion of ''Melaleuca'' in South Florida |journal=Journal of Aquatic Plant Management |date=1992 |volume=30 |pages=62–65 |url=https://apms.org/wp-content/uploads/japm-30-02-062.pdf|access-date=19 October 2024}}</ref>

This tree takes over [[Cladium|sawgrass]] marshes in the Everglades turning the area into a swamp.<ref name=Zedler04>{{cite journal | last1 = Zedler | first1 = J. B. | last2 = Kercher | first2 = Suzanne | year = 2004 | title = Causes and consequences of invasive plants in wetlands: Opportunities, opportunists, and outcomes | journal = Critical Reviews in Plant Sciences | volume = 23 | issue = 5| pages = 431–52 | doi = 10.1080/07352680490514673 | bibcode = 2004CRvPS..23..431Z | s2cid = 1837791 }}</ref> ''Melaleuca'' causes severe ecological impacts, including displacing native species, modification of [[hydrology]], alteration of soil resources, reducing native habitat value and changing the fire regime.<ref name="Mazz97">{{cite web |last1=Mazzotti |first1=Frank J. |last2=Center |first2=Ted D. |last3=Dray |first3=F. Allen |last4=Thayer |first4=Dan |title=Ecological Consequences of Invasion by ''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' in South Florida Wetlands: Paradise Damaged, not Lost |url=http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/UW123 |publisher=University of Florida |pages=1–5 |access-date=19 October 2024 |archive-date=2 May 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150502210344/http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/uw123 }}</ref>

An experiment comparing the quantity of seeds held in the canopies of ''Melaleuca'' trees in Australia and Southern Florida found that the viability and amount of seeds found in Australia were lower when compared to those in Florida.<ref name="Ram02">{{cite journal |last1=Rayamajhi |first1=Min B. |last2=Van |first2=Thai K. |last3=Centre |first3=Ted. D. |last4=Goolsby |first4=John A. |last5=Pratt |first5=Paul D. |last6=Racelis |first6=Alex |title=Biological Attributes of The Canopy-held Melaleuca Seeds in Australia and Florida, U.S. |journal=Journal of Aquatic Plant Management |date=2002 |volume=40 |pages=87–91 |url=https://apms.org/wp-content/uploads/japm-40-02-087.pdf|access-date=19 October 2024}}</ref>

The release from natural enemies will cause the invasive exotic plant to evolve, improving its performance in the new area.<ref name="Hierro">{{cite journal |last1=Hierro |first1=José L. |last2=Maron |first2=John L. |last3=Callaway |first3=Ragan M. |title=A biogeographical approach to plant invasions: the importance of studying exotics in their introduced and native range |journal=Journal of Ecology |date=2005 |volume=93 |issue=1 |pages=5–15 |doi=10.1111/j.0022-0477.2004.00953.x |bibcode=2005JEcol..93....5H |url=https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/j.0022-0477.2004.00953.x |access-date=19 October 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This idea is supported by the results of a study on ''Melaleuca'' done by Pratt et al. (2005) showing that damage by herbivores reduced success in the following season as the reproductive structures declined by 80% with 54% less fruits. Biocontrol agents that have been released in Florida are the ''[[Oxyops vitiosa]]'' (weevil) and ''Boreioglycapsis'' (melaleuca psyllid). These insects are native to Australia and serve to reduce the growth and reproduction of ''M. quinquenervia'' by feeding on young expanding leaves and phloem of the tree.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Wheeler|first=G.S.|title=Chemotype variation of the weed ''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' influences the biomass and fecundity of the biological control agent Oxyops vitiosa|journal=Biological Control|year=2005|volume=36|issue=2|pages=121–128|doi=10.1016/j.biocontrol.2005.10.005|url=https://naldc-legacy.nal.usda.gov/naldc/download.xhtml?id=1800&content=PDF|url-access=subscription}}{{dead link|date=June 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Padovan|first=A.|author2=Keszei, A. |author3=Koellner, T. G. |author4=Degenhardt, J. |author5=Foley, W. J. |title=The molecular basis of host plant selection in ''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' by a successful biological control agent|journal=Phytochemistry|year=2010|volume=71|issue=11–12|pages=1237–1244|doi=10.1016/j.phytochem.2010.05.013|pmid=20554297|bibcode=2010PChem..71.1237P }}</ref>

Punk tree is known for its capability to withstand [[flood]]s and [[drought]]s.<ref name="Serbesoff-King" /> If there is a canopy gap created by a flood or some other disturbance ''Melaleuca'' will establish to make use of the extra light.<ref name="Zedler04" /> In physically disturbed sites, flourishing invaders have high colonisation abilities.<ref name="Lake04" /> For example, ''Melaleuca'' is constantly thinning itself of small branches and twigs and this causes many seeds to fall all the time along with the litter,<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Van | first1 = T. K. | last2 = Rayachhetry | first2 = M. B. | last3 = Center | first3 = T. D. | last4 = Pratt | first4 = P. D. | year = 2002 | title = Litter dynamics and phenology of ''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' in South Florida | journal = Journal of Aquatic Plant Management | volume = 40 | pages = 22–27 }}</ref> so it is always dispersing its potential offspring. ''Melaleuca'' is also capable of living in disturbed habitats such as improved pasture, [[idle farmland]],<ref name="Mazz97" /> and canal affected areas. The climate in south Florida is similar to that in its native Australia, beginning with geographic locations at [[26th parallel north|latitude 26º N]] about halfway between Lake Okeechobee and the tip of mainland Florida; in Australia the [[26th parallel south|latitude 26º S]] lies just north of Brisbane in south Queensland.

Both regions have subtropical to tropical climate. As a result of this, ''Melaleuca'' has almost been pre-adapted for south Florida. Fire thrives in these environments and seed dispersal is displaced when fire occurs.{{R|TURNER}} ''Melaleuca'' bloom five times throughout the year, with individual branches supporting three out of the five. Each flower part can drop about 30–70 small seed capsules which can be viable for almost ten years. It was determined that each capsule contained about 200–300 seeds, dropping rapidly and can be found 170 m from the source tree.  The seeds of ''M. quinquenervia'' appear to be well adapted to wet/dry seasonal climates and can even germinate underwater on soil substrate.{{R|TURNER}}

Recent studies comparing specific leaf area of invasive exotic plants with exotic non-invasive plants and native plants in relation to disturbances have shown that invasive have a larger specific leaf area than the other plants.<ref name=Lake04>{{cite journal |vauthors=Lake JC, Leishman MR |year=2004|title= Invasion success of exotic plants in natural ecosystems: the role of disturbance, plant attributes and freedom from herbivores |journal=Biological Conservation |volume=117|pages=215–26 |doi=10.1016/S0006-3207(03)00294-5 |issue=2 |bibcode=2004BCons.117..215L }}</ref> This allows for faster growth, these results held up by many supporting studies have allowed Lake and Leishman to infer that invasive species are so successful because of their skill for fast growth, and greater capacity to capture and retain space. ''Melaleuca'' has definitely been shown to have these traits, such as in the Everglades where the ''Melaleuca'' population increased 50-fold between the early 1970s and the late 1990s.<ref name=Mazz97/>

==Chemistry==
[[File:Chemotypes found in Melaleuca quinquenervia.svg|thumb|Chemotypes found in ''Melaleuca quinquenervia'']]
''M. quinquenervia'' have been shown to occur in distinct chemical forms. These forms or chemotypes are characterised by the organic compounds [[terpene]]s. Chemotype 1 has acyclic foliar terpenes, with concentrations of sesquiterpene E-[[nerolidol]] 74–95% of total oil and also monoterpene [[linalool]].<ref name="Ireland2002">{{cite journal|last=Ireland|first=B.F. |author2=D.B. Hibbert |author3=R.J. Goldsack |author4=J.C. Doran |author5=J.J. Brophy|title=Chemical variation in the leaf essential oil of ''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' (Cav.) S.T. Blake|journal=Biochemical Systematics and Ecology|year=2002|pages=457–470|doi=10.1016/s0305-1978(01)00112-0 |volume=30 |issue=5 |bibcode=2002BioSE..30..457I }}</ref> Chemotype 2 has high concentration of cyclic foliar terpenes, in particular sesquiterpene [[viridiflorol]] with 13-66% of total oil. Chemotype 2 also includes monoterpenes 1,8-[[cineole]] and α-[[terpineol]].<ref name="Ireland2002" />

[[Grandinin]] is an ellagitannin also found in leaves of ''M. quinquenervia''.<ref name=Moharram>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1002/ptr.1214 | volume=17 | title=Polyphenols of Melaleuca quinquenervia leaves - pharmacological studies of grandinin | year=2003 | journal=Phytotherapy Research | pages=767–773 | last1 = Moharram | first1 = F. A. | issue=7 | pmid=12916075| s2cid=45936055 }}</ref>

==Uses==
The paper-like bark is used traditionally for making [[coolamon (vessel)|coolamon]]s and shelters and for wrapping baked food and lining ground ovens.<ref name=EJ93/> The nectar is extracted traditionally by washing in coolamons of water which is subsequently consumed as a [[beverage]]. The scented flower also produces a light to dark amber [[honey]] depending on the district. It is strongly flavoured and candies readily. It is not regarded as a high-quality honey but nevertheless is popular.<ref>Cribb, A.B. & J.W., Useful Wild Plants in Australia, Collins 1982, p. 23, {{ISBN|0-00-636397-0}}.</ref>

''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' is sometimes used as a [[bonsai]].<ref name="ANBG">{{cite web |title=Australian Plants as Bonsai - ''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' |url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/bonsai/images-06-captions/28-Melaleuca-quinquenervia-RH-e-137-3779_IMG.html |publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens |access-date=15 May 2020}}</ref>

The timber is tolerant of being soaked and is used in fences.<ref name=Hallstreet/>

''Melaleuca quinquenervia'' is often used as a street tree or planted in public parks and gardens, especially in Sydney.<ref name=Hallmel>{{cite book |title=Melaleucas: A Field and Garden Guide|last=Halliday |first=Ivan |year=2004 |publisher=New Holland Press |location=Sydney |isbn=1-876334-98-3 |page=238}}</ref> In its native Australia, it is excellent as a windbreak, screening tree and food source for a wide range of local insect and bird species.<ref name=EJ93/><ref>{{cite book |title=Attracting Wildlife to Your Garden |last=Elliot |first=Rodger |year=1994 |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Melbourne |isbn=0-85091-628-3 |page=58}}</ref> It can tolerate waterlogged soils.<ref name=Hallstreet>{{cite book |title=A Field Guide to Australian Trees |last=Halliday |first=Ivan |year=1989 |publisher=Hamlyn Australia |isbn=0-947334-08-4 |page=262 |location=Melbourne}}</ref>
